title: Tallinn to Helsinki: ferry, flight or day trip – how to choose
desc: Everything you need to cross the Gulf of Finland: ferry companies, travel times, tickets, and how to do Helsinki as a day trip from Tallinn.
body:
Tallinn and Helsinki are only about 80 km apart, and the ferry between them is one of the busiest sea routes in Europe. Millions of people cross every year for work, shopping and short city breaks. Here is how to choose the right option.

Ferry: the default choice

Three companies run the route all year: Tallink (fast ships such as Megastar and MyStar, about 2 hours), Viking Line (about 2.5 hours) and Eckerö Line (often the cheapest, about 2–2.5 hours). There are many sailings a day in each direction.

  • Book online in advance – fares change with demand, and Friday evenings, Sunday afternoons and holidays are the most expensive.
  • Foot passengers can usually check in by scanning the ticket at the gate; arrive 30–45 minutes before departure.
  • Cars need to arrive earlier and cost more – useful if you continue to Lapland or around Finland.
  • In Tallinn, most ships leave from the Old City Harbour (terminals A and D), a 15–20 minute walk from the Old Town. In Helsinki, check whether your ship arrives at West Harbour (Länsisatama) or the South/Katajanokka terminals.

Flying

There is a short flight between the two cities, but once you add airport transfers and security, it is rarely faster than the ferry. It can make sense when you connect to a long-haul flight from Helsinki – compare flight prices with the ferry before deciding.

Helsinki as a day trip from Tallinn

A day trip works well: take a morning ferry, spend 6–8 hours in the city and return in the evening. A simple route:

  1. Walk from the harbour to the Market Square and the Old Market Hall.
  2. See Senate Square and the Helsinki Cathedral, then the Uspenski Cathedral.
  3. Take the public ferry (part of the HSL network) to Suomenlinna sea fortress.
  4. Finish with the Esplanadi park, the Oodi library and the Temppeliaukio rock church.

Museum tickets and boat tours are easy to book online so you don't waste time in queues.

Day trip to Tallinn from Helsinki

Many Finns do the reverse trip. Tallinn's medieval Old Town starts a short walk from the harbour, so you can see the Town Hall Square, Toompea hill and the viewing platforms in a few hours. Read our Tallinn budget guide for details.

Tips

  • Bring your passport or EU ID card – both countries are in Schengen, but ferry companies can ask for ID.
  • Your phone works in both countries with an EU SIM; visitors from outside the EU can use an eSIM.
  • If your ferry arrives late at night, a pre-booked transfer is easier than looking for a taxi.

title: Tallinn Airport to the city centre: tram, bus, taxi and transfer
desc: How to get from Lennart Meri Tallinn Airport to the Old Town and the harbour – the cheapest and fastest options explained.
body:
Tallinn Airport (Lennart Meri, TLL) is one of the closest airports to a capital city centre in Europe – only about 4 km from the Old Town. Getting into town is quick and cheap.

Tram 4 – the easiest option

Tram line 4 stops right next to the terminal and goes to the city centre (Viru Keskus and Hobujaama stops are next to the Old Town) in about 15–20 minutes. Trams run frequently from early morning until around midnight.

Bus 2

City bus 2 also connects the airport with the centre and continues to the passenger port (A-terminal). It is handy if you are going straight to the Helsinki ferry – see our Tallinn–Helsinki guide.

Tickets

  • The simplest way to pay is to tap a contactless bank card or phone on the validator when you board – it buys a time ticket automatically.
  • You can also buy tickets in the Pilet.ee app or a Ühiskaart travel card.
  • Registered Tallinn residents travel free, but visitors must pay.

Taxi and ride-hailing

Taxis wait outside arrivals, and ride-hailing apps such as Bolt (an Estonian company) work well. The ride to the Old Town takes about 10–15 minutes. Check the price on the sticker in the taxi window before you get in.

Pre-booked transfer

For families, late-night arrivals or groups with luggage, a pre-booked transfer with a fixed price and a meeting sign is the most relaxed option.

Renting a car

Rental desks are in the arrivals hall. A car is not needed in the city, but it is great for day trips to Lahemaa National Park, Pärnu or Tartu. Compare car rental prices in advance – it is usually cheaper than booking on the spot.

Planning more? Read Tallinn on a budget and find cheap flights to Tallinn.

title: Helsinki Airport to the city centre: train, bus and taxi
desc: How to get from Helsinki-Vantaa Airport to Helsinki centre: the airport train, buses, taxis and transfers, with ticket tips.
body:
Helsinki-Vantaa Airport (HEL) is about 20 km north of the city centre. Public transport is easy, frequent and reasonably priced.

The airport train (I and P lines)

The Ring Rail Line stops in a station directly under the airport. Both the I and P trains go to Helsinki Central Station – they just travel around the loop in opposite directions, and the trip takes about 30 minutes. Trains run every 10 minutes or so for most of the day.

Tickets

  • The airport is in HSL zone C, so you need an ABC ticket to reach the centre.
  • Buy it in the HSL app, from ticket machines at the station, or pay with a contactless bank card at the readers on the platform.
  • If you will use public transport a lot, a day ticket for zones ABC can be better value.

Buses

Bus 600 runs from the airport to the Railway Square in the centre and takes longer than the train, but it is useful for stops along the way and at night.

Taxi and ride-hailing

Taxis are available outside arrivals; the ride to the centre takes about 25–35 minutes. Finnish taxis are not cheap, so check fixed-price options in the taxi apps or at the taxi rank.

Pre-booked transfer

With children, lots of luggage or a late flight, a pre-booked transfer with a fixed price is the least stressful choice.

Continuing your trip

  • To Tallinn: take the train or a taxi to the harbour and catch a ferry – see Tallinn to Helsinki.
  • To Lapland: fly to Rovaniemi, or take the night train from Helsinki – read our Lapland guide.
  • To explore Finland by road: compare car rentals at the airport.

More ideas in Helsinki in 2–3 days.

title: Riga to Tallinn: bus, train, car or flight
desc: How to travel between Riga and Tallinn: comfortable coaches, the train with a change in Valga, driving the Via Baltica, and short flights.
body:
Riga and Tallinn are about 310 km apart, and many travellers visit both capitals on one trip. Here are the options, from cheapest to most flexible.

Bus – the most popular option

Comfortable coaches (Lux Express, FlixBus and others) run many times a day between the two bus stations and take about 4–4.5 hours. Most have Wi-Fi, power sockets and screens. Book online for the best fares; early-morning and late-evening departures are often cheapest.

Train with a change in Valga

There is no direct fast train yet (the new Rail Baltica line is still being built), but you can travel by rail: a Latvian train from Riga to Valga, then an Estonian Elron train from Valga to Tallinn. It takes longer than the bus, but it is a scenic, relaxed way to travel. Check the timetables of both operators so the connection works.

By car

The Via Baltica road (A1 in Latvia, route 4 in Estonia) takes about 4 hours. A car lets you stop in Pärnu, Estonia's summer capital, or in the Gauja National Park near Sigulda. If you rent a car in one country and return it in the other, check the one-way fee – compare rental offers before booking.

Flight

The flight is about 50 minutes and can be useful for connections, but it is rarely faster door to door than the bus. Compare flight prices anyway – sometimes there are good deals.

Which should you choose?

  • Lowest price and simplest: bus.
  • Most scenic and relaxed: train via Valga.
  • Most flexible, with stops on the way: car.

Read our guides to Riga, Tallinn and Vilnius to plan the whole Baltic trip.

title: Best time to visit the Baltics: a month-by-month guide
desc: When to visit Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania: white nights, Christmas markets, snowy winters and the best months for good prices.
body:
Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania have four very different seasons. The best time depends on what you want – long summer days, festivals, or quiet, cheap city breaks.

Summer (June–August)

The most popular season. Days are very long – around midsummer it barely gets dark – and the weather is usually 18–25 °C. Midsummer (23–24 June: Jaanipäev, Līgo and Joninės) is the biggest holiday of the year, with bonfires and festivals in the countryside. Beaches in Pärnu, Jūrmala and Palanga are busy. Book flights and hotels early.

Autumn (September–October)

September is often still mild, and prices drop after the school holidays. October brings autumn colours in the national parks and quiet old towns. A great time for city breaks.

Winter (November–March)

Short days and frost, but beautiful: Christmas markets in Tallinn, Riga and Vilnius from late November, snow-covered old towns and cosy cafés. January to March is usually the cheapest time for flights and hotels. Bring warm clothes and good shoes.

Spring (April–May)

Days get longer quickly, parks turn green in May, and the summer crowds have not arrived yet. Good value and good weather for walking.

Quick summary

  • Best weather: June–August.
  • Best value: January–March and October–November.
  • Christmas atmosphere: late November–December.
  • Balanced choice: May and September.

Plan your trip

Use the budget wheel in the Tripwise app to see which cities you can reach for your budget, find cheap flights, and book tours and tickets in advance in high season. Then read our guides to Tallinn, Riga and Vilnius, and how to move between them in Riga to Tallinn.

title: Tallinn on a budget: a practical 3-day guide
desc: Where to stay, what to see and how to save money in Tallinn, Estonia's medieval capital.
body:
Tallinn packs a UNESCO-listed Old Town, a creative harbour district and a wild Baltic coastline into a city you can cross by tram in twenty minutes. It is also one of the easier Nordic-Baltic capitals to visit on a modest budget, if you plan a little.

When to go

June to August brings long white nights and open-air festivals, but also cruise-ship crowds and the highest hotel prices. May and September are the sweet spot: mild weather, fewer people, lower rates. December is magical thanks to the Christmas market on Town Hall Square, though days are short and cold.

Where to stay

  • Old Town – unbeatable atmosphere, but the most expensive and noisy at weekends.
  • Kesklinn (city centre) and Rotermann – modern hotels a five-minute walk from the Old Town, often 20–30% cheaper.
  • Kalamaja and Telliskivi – wooden houses, cafés and the Telliskivi Creative City; good value apartments and a local feel.
  • Kadriorg – quiet, green, next to the park and the art museum; ideal for families.

Getting around

Tallinn Airport is only 4 km from the centre and tram line 4 runs straight into town, so you rarely need a taxi. Public transport tickets are bought with a contactless bank card on board. If you arrive late at night with luggage or children, a pre-booked airport transfer saves stress. For day trips to Lahemaa National Park or the beaches of Pärnu, renting a car is the most flexible option.

What to see

  • Toompea hill viewpoints (Kohtuotsa and Patkuli) – free and best at sunset.
  • St Olaf's Church tower and the Town Hall tower for views over the red roofs.
  • Kadriorg Palace and park, and the KUMU art museum.
  • Seaplane Harbour (Lennusadam) – a submarine, icebreaker and seaplanes under one roof.
  • Telliskivi Creative City and the Balti Jaama market for street food and vintage shops.

Museum and attraction tickets can be booked online in advance, which helps on busy summer days. Prefer exploring at your own pace? A self-guided audio tour of the Old Town costs less than a group tour.

Money-saving tips

  • Eat your main meal at lunch: many restaurants offer a "päevapraad" (daily lunch special) at a fraction of the dinner price.
  • Tap water is excellent – carry a bottle.
  • Walk: the Old Town, Kalamaja and the harbour are all within 25 minutes on foot.
  • A day trip to Helsinki by ferry takes about two hours each way – watch for midweek ferry deals.

Staying connected

Estonia is famously digital and free Wi-Fi is everywhere, but if you are coming from outside the EU, an eSIM data plan is usually far cheaper than roaming.

title: A weekend in Riga: Art Nouveau, markets and good value
desc: How to spend 48 hours in Riga, Latvia: neighbourhoods, sights, food and transport tips.
body:
Riga is the largest city in the Baltics and one of Europe's most underrated weekend breaks. It combines a compact medieval centre with the world's finest collection of Art Nouveau buildings and a huge food market housed in former Zeppelin hangars.

Day 1: Old Riga and the market

Start at the House of the Blackheads and Town Hall Square, then wander to St Peter's Church – its tower lift gives the best panorama of the city. Continue past the Three Brothers and the Swedish Gate. In the afternoon, head to the Central Market: five pavilions of smoked fish, cheese, rye bread and seasonal berries. It is the cheapest place in town for a picnic lunch.

Day 2: Art Nouveau and the parks

Alberta and Elizabetes streets are lined with ornate façades by Mikhail Eisenstein and others. The Art Nouveau Museum shows a restored apartment from 1903. Afterwards, walk through Bastejkalns park along the canal to the Freedom Monument. In the evening, try a Latvian beer hall or the bars of the Miera iela district.

Where to stay

  • Old Riga (Vecrīga) – walk everywhere, but check that your room isn't above a bar.
  • Centrs / Quiet Centre – the Art Nouveau quarter; elegant and quieter, often better value.
  • Ķīpsala – across the river with skyline views; good for families and drivers.

Getting there and around

Riga Airport (RIX) is the main Baltic hub, with low-cost routes across Europe – compare flight prices across airlines and dates, as midweek departures are often cheaper. Bus 22 links the airport and the centre in about 30 minutes; a pre-booked transfer is handy for late arrivals. Jūrmala's beaches are 30 minutes away by train, and a rental car opens up Gauja National Park and Sigulda castle.

Budget tips

  • Business-lunch menus on weekdays offer two or three courses at low prices.
  • Many churches and the Art Nouveau streets are free to explore.
  • Buy public transport tickets in advance rather than from the driver.

For guided walks, museum tickets and day trips, see the activities available in Riga.

title: Helsinki in 2–3 days: design, saunas and islands
desc: A practical Helsinki guide: where to stay, sauna culture, Suomenlinna and how to save money in Finland.
body:
Helsinki is relaxed, walkable and surrounded by sea. Finland has a reputation for being expensive, but with the right choices a few days here can be surprisingly affordable.

Top experiences

  • Suomenlinna – a UNESCO sea fortress on islands, reached by the regular city ferry from Market Square (included in a public transport ticket).
  • Public saunas – Löyly, Allas Sea Pool and the traditional Kotiharjun sauna. Swimming in the sea afterwards is part of the experience, even in winter.
  • Design District – boutiques, galleries and the Design Museum south of Esplanadi.
  • Temppeliaukio rock church and the Oodi central library, a striking modern building that is free to enter.
  • Old Market Hall for salmon soup and Finnish pastries.

Where to stay

  • Kamppi and Kluuvi – central, close to the bus and train stations.
  • Punavuori – the design district, with cafés and restaurants.
  • Kallio – the former working-class district, now lively and usually cheaper.

Transport

The train from Helsinki-Vantaa Airport to the centre takes about 30 minutes; buy an HSL ticket for zones ABC. A day ticket covers trams, metro, buses and the Suomenlinna ferry. Travelling with lots of luggage? Book an airport transfer in advance. Nuuksio National Park and the old town of Porvoo make great day trips – a car rental makes them easier.

Save money in Helsinki

  • Lunch buffets ("lounas") on weekdays are the best-value meal in Finland.
  • Supermarkets like Lidl and K-Market sell good ready-made food.
  • Many museums have free entry on certain evenings – check before you go.
  • Combine with Tallinn: ferries cross the Gulf of Finland many times a day.

Book museum tickets and tours online, and get an eSIM if you're visiting from outside the EU.

title: Lapland in winter: how to plan a Rovaniemi trip without overpaying
desc: Northern lights, husky safaris and Santa Claus Village: timing, budget and booking tips for Finnish Lapland.
body:
Rovaniemi, on the Arctic Circle, is the gateway to Finnish Lapland. Between December and March it offers snow, husky and reindeer safaris and – with luck – the northern lights. It is popular, so planning ahead makes a big difference to the price.

When to go

  • Late November – December: Christmas atmosphere, but only a few hours of daylight and the highest prices around the holidays.
  • January – February: deep snow and cold (often −15 to −30 °C), fewer families, lower prices. Good aurora chances on clear nights.
  • March: longer days, sunshine on snow, still good aurora odds – great value.

Getting there

Rovaniemi has an airport with direct winter flights from many European cities, plus domestic flights from Helsinki. The overnight Santa Claus Express train from Helsinki is a scenic alternative. Flight prices rise sharply for Christmas dates – compare dates a few months ahead.

What to do

  • Santa Claus Village – free to enter, right on the Arctic Circle line.
  • Husky and reindeer safaris – book early for December.
  • Northern lights tours that drive away from city lights when the sky is clear.
  • Arktikum museum for Arctic science and Sámi culture.

Popular activities and safaris sell out in high season. If you want to chase the aurora yourself, a rental car with winter tyres gives you freedom – drive carefully and watch for reindeer on the road.

Packing and budget tips

  • Layer: thermal base layer, fleece, insulated jacket, warm boots and mittens. Many safaris include thermal overalls.
  • Self-catering apartments and cabins cut food costs considerably.
  • Stay a few kilometres outside the centre for darker skies and lower rates.

title: Barcelona for first-timers: neighbourhoods, sights and smart booking
desc: Plan your first trip to Barcelona: which area to stay in, how to skip lines at Gaudí sights and save money.
body:
Barcelona mixes beaches, Gaudí architecture, Gothic lanes and some of Europe's best food. It is also very busy, so a few booking tricks make a real difference.

Where to stay

  • Eixample – central, safe, full of Modernista buildings and close to the metro. The best all-round choice.
  • Gràcia – village feel, squares and local bars; slightly cheaper.
  • Gothic Quarter and El Born – atmospheric but crowded and noisy at night.
  • Poblenou – near the beach, quieter, newer hotels.

Must-see sights (and why to pre-book)

The Sagrada Família, Park Güell, Casa Batlló and La Pedrera all use timed tickets, and the best slots sell out days ahead in high season. Buying tickets online in advance avoids long queues and disappointment. Montjuïc, the Bunkers del Carmel viewpoint and the beaches are free.

Getting around

The Aerobús and the L9 metro link El Prat airport with the city. A pre-booked transfer is worth it for families or late flights. Inside the city, the metro is fast; a multi-trip T-casual card is cheaper than single tickets.

Food on a budget

  • The "menú del día" at lunchtime: usually three courses with a drink at a fixed price.
  • Skip restaurants on La Rambla; walk a few streets away for better value.
  • Visit La Boqueria early, then try smaller markets like Santa Caterina.

Safety tip

Pickpocketing is common on the metro and in crowded areas. Keep your phone and wallet in front pockets and use a cross-body bag.

Find cheap flights to Barcelona by staying flexible on dates – Tuesday and Wednesday departures are often the cheapest.

title: Rome in three days: an efficient itinerary
desc: See the Colosseum, Vatican and Trastevere in three days, with tips on tickets, transport and where to stay.
body:
Rome rewards walkers: almost all the great sights sit within a few kilometres of each other. Three days is enough for the highlights if you book the big-ticket sites ahead.

Day 1: Ancient Rome

Start early at the Colosseum, then continue to the Roman Forum and Palatine Hill (one combined ticket, timed entry). In the afternoon, walk to Piazza Venezia, the Capitoline Hill and the Pantheon. End with dinner in the Monti district.

Day 2: Vatican and Prati

The Vatican Museums and Sistine Chapel are among the busiest attractions in the world – pre-booked skip-the-line tickets save hours. St Peter's Basilica is free but has a security queue; go early or late. Have lunch in the Prati district, then cross the river to Castel Sant'Angelo.

Day 3: Piazzas and Trastevere

Trevi Fountain at 8 am, the Spanish Steps, Piazza Navona and Campo de' Fiori. Spend the evening in Trastevere for trattorias and street life. If you prefer to explore independently, a self-guided audio tour adds context without a group.

Where to stay

  • Centro Storico – walk to everything, higher prices.
  • Monti – near the Colosseum, charming and central.
  • Prati – near the Vatican, calmer and good value.
  • Trastevere – lively evenings, cobbled lanes.

Practical tips

  • The Leonardo Express train links Fiumicino airport and Termini station; a private transfer is often similar in price for three or four people.
  • Drink from the free "nasoni" water fountains around the city.
  • Cover shoulders and knees for churches.
  • Many state museums are free on the first Sunday of the month – expect crowds.

title: eSIM for travel: how it works and how much you can save
desc: A simple explanation of travel eSIMs, which phones support them and how they compare with roaming.
body:
An eSIM is a digital SIM card built into your phone. Instead of buying a plastic SIM at the airport, you install a data plan by scanning a QR code or tapping a link – often before you leave home.

Why use a travel eSIM?

  • Cost – roaming outside your home region can be very expensive; local or regional eSIM data packs are usually much cheaper.
  • Convenience – you're online the moment you land, for maps, taxis and messages.
  • Keep your number – your normal SIM stays active for calls and SMS (e.g. bank codes), while the eSIM handles data.

Does my phone support eSIM?

Most iPhones from the XS/XR onwards, recent Google Pixel phones and many Samsung Galaxy S, Z and newer A models support eSIM. The phone must also be unlocked from your carrier. On iPhone, look for "Add eSIM" in Settings → Mobile Data; on Android, check Settings → Connections → SIM manager.

How to set it up

  1. Choose a plan for your destination country or region (e.g. Europe, Asia, global).
  2. Install the eSIM while you still have Wi-Fi – ideally the day before departure.
  3. On arrival, switch mobile data to the eSIM and turn on data roaming for that line.

Tips

  • Regional plans are good value if you visit several countries.
  • Most travel eSIMs are data-only; use WhatsApp or Telegram for calls.
  • Don't delete the eSIM until you've used up or no longer need the plan.

You can browse eSIM plans for 200+ countries and install one in a few minutes.

title: Flight delayed or cancelled? Your rights to compensation in Europe
desc: EU Regulation 261/2004 explained simply: when you can claim up to €600 for a delayed or cancelled flight.
body:
Under EU Regulation 261/2004, passengers can receive between €250 and €600 per person when a flight arrives more than three hours late, is cancelled at short notice or is overbooked. Many travellers never claim.

Which flights are covered?

  • All flights departing from an airport in the EU (plus Iceland, Norway and Switzerland), with any airline.
  • Flights arriving in the EU when operated by an EU-based airline.
  • The UK has an equivalent rule (UK261) for flights to and from the UK.

How much?

  • €250 for flights up to 1,500 km.
  • €400 for flights within the EU over 1,500 km, and other flights of 1,500–3,500 km.
  • €600 for flights over 3,500 km (may be reduced by half if the delay is 3–4 hours).

When airlines don't have to pay

Compensation is not due for "extraordinary circumstances" such as severe weather, air traffic control restrictions, security threats or some strikes not involving airline staff. Technical problems usually do not count as extraordinary.

Your other rights

Regardless of compensation, after a long delay the airline must provide meals and refreshments, and hotel accommodation if you are stuck overnight. Keep your receipts.

How to claim

  1. Keep your boarding pass and booking confirmation; note the actual arrival time.
  2. Submit a claim directly to the airline, or
  3. use a claims service that handles the process for a share of the compensation, only if successful – for example AirHelp.

Claims can often be made for flights several years in the past, depending on the country.

title: How to find cheap flights: 10 tips that actually work
desc: Practical, honest tips for finding lower airfares: flexible dates, nearby airports, price alerts and more.
body:
There's no magic trick for cheap flights, but a few habits consistently save money.

  1. Be flexible with dates. Moving your trip by a day or two often makes the biggest difference. Midweek departures are usually cheaper than Fridays and Sundays.
  2. Compare many airlines at once. A flight search engine shows low-cost and full-service carriers side by side.
  3. Check nearby airports. Tallinn, Riga and Helsinki are close to each other – one may be much cheaper than the others for the same destination.
  4. Set a price alert. Prices move up and down; the Tripwise app can watch a route and message you in Telegram when it drops.
  5. Book at the right time. For European flights, one to three months ahead is usually a good window; for holidays and long-haul, book earlier.
  6. Look at the total price. Low-cost fares exclude bags and seat selection – compare the final cost.
  7. Consider one-ways. Two one-way tickets on different airlines can beat a return.
  8. Travel light. A cabin-bag-only trip opens up the cheapest fares.
  9. Be open to destinations. If you just want a weekend away, search by budget instead of city – the Tripwise budget wheel does exactly that.
  10. Know your rights. If your flight is badly delayed, you may be owed compensation – see our guide.

title: Vilnius in a weekend: baroque streets, Užupis and great value
desc: A compact guide to Lithuania's capital: what to see, where to stay and how to keep costs low.
body:
Vilnius has one of the largest surviving medieval old towns in Northern and Eastern Europe, and it is UNESCO-listed. It is full of baroque churches, courtyards and cafés, and prices are usually lower than in the Nordic capitals.

What to see

  • Old Town – Cathedral Square, Pilies Street, the Gate of Dawn and St Anne's Church, a gothic gem.
  • Gediminas Tower – climb or take the funicular for a view over the red roofs.
  • Užupis – the self-declared "republic" of artists, with its constitution displayed on a wall in many languages.
  • Trakai – an island castle 30 minutes away by bus or train, perfect for a half-day trip.

Where to stay

Stay in or next to the Old Town to walk everywhere. Naujamiestis, just west of it, has newer hotels and apartments at lower prices.

Getting around

Vilnius Airport is close to the centre, about 15 minutes by bus or train. For late arrivals, a pre-booked transfer is simple. To see Trakai, the Hill of Crosses or the Curonian Spit, rent a car: Lithuanian roads are good and distances short.

Budget tips

  • Try cepelinai (potato dumplings) and šaltibarščiai (cold pink beet soup) in local canteens for a cheap, filling meal.
  • Many churches are free to visit.
  • Use public transport apps or contactless payment instead of taxis.

Find cheap flights to Vilnius and museum tickets and tours before you go.

title: Prague on a budget: how to enjoy the city without tourist prices
desc: Practical tips for Prague: the best areas, sights worth paying for, and how to avoid tourist traps.
body:
Prague is one of Europe's most beautiful cities and still good value if you avoid the busiest tourist spots for eating and exchanging money.

The classic route

Start at Prague Castle and St Vitus Cathedral early in the morning, walk down through Malá Strana to Charles Bridge, and continue to the Old Town Square and the Astronomical Clock. The castle grounds are free; the main buildings need a ticket.

Beyond the centre

  • Vyšehrad – a quiet fortress with river views and a historic cemetery.
  • Letná Park – a beer garden with one of the best views of the bridges.
  • Vinohrady and Žižkov – local cafés and pubs with lower prices.

Money tips

  • Pay by card or withdraw from bank ATMs; avoid exchange offices with "0% commission" signs and bad rates.
  • Lunch menus ("polední menu") on weekdays are the cheapest way to eat well.
  • A public transport ticket covers trams, metro and the funicular to Petřín Hill.

Getting there

Bus 59 and the Airport Express connect Václav Havel Airport with the metro and the main station. Prefer a direct ride? Book a private transfer. Use a flight comparison to find the cheapest days to fly.

For castle tickets, river cruises and day trips to Český Krumlov or Kutná Hora, see tours and activities.

title: Lisbon for first-timers: neighbourhoods, trams and day trips
desc: Where to stay in Lisbon, how to get around the hills, and the best day trips to Sintra and Cascais.
body:
Lisbon spreads over seven hills above the Tagus river. Sunny viewpoints, tiled façades and pastéis de nata make it one of Europe's favourite city breaks.

Where to stay

  • Baixa and Chiado – central and flat between the hills, close to everything.
  • Alfama – the oldest district, full of character and fado bars, but steep.
  • Príncipe Real – elegant, quieter, with gardens and boutiques.
  • Cais do Sodré – lively at night and next to the train to Cascais.

Getting around

Comfortable shoes are essential. Trams, funiculars and the metro make the hills easier; a rechargeable transport card is cheaper than single tickets. The metro runs from the airport to the centre in about 25 minutes. A pre-booked transfer helps with luggage.

Must-sees

  • Belém: Jerónimos Monastery and the tower by the river.
  • Miradouros (viewpoints) like Senhora do Monte and Santa Catarina – free and best at sunset.
  • LX Factory and the Time Out Market for food.

Day trips

Sintra's palaces are 40 minutes away by train; go early on a weekday and book palace tickets in advance. Cascais has beaches reachable by train along the coast. To explore the Algarve or the Alentejo, rent a car.

title: Istanbul in four days: two continents, one itinerary
desc: A practical Istanbul itinerary with the main sights, ferries, food tips and where to stay.
body:
Istanbul straddles Europe and Asia across the Bosphorus. It's huge, so a plan by area saves a lot of time.

Day 1: Sultanahmet

Hagia Sophia, the Blue Mosque, the Basilica Cistern and the Hippodrome are all within walking distance. Dress modestly for mosques; women need a headscarf. Visit early, and avoid prayer times.

Day 2: Topkapı and the bazaars

Topkapı Palace deserves half a day. Then walk to the Grand Bazaar and the Spice Bazaar. Haggling is normal, so start lower and stay friendly.

Day 3: Beyoğlu and Galata

Walk down İstiklal Avenue to the Galata Tower and Karaköy's cafés. In the evening, take a ferry across the Bosphorus – one of the best-value views in the city.

Day 4: The Asian side

Ferry to Kadıköy for its market, street food and relaxed atmosphere, and walk along the Moda seafront.

Practical tips

  • Get an Istanbulkart for trams, metro, buses and ferries.
  • Istanbul Airport is far from the centre (about an hour); the metro or a pre-booked transfer is easier than haggling with taxis.
  • Book a Bosphorus cruise or skip-the-line tickets for the busiest sights.
  • An eSIM saves money if you are coming from outside Türkiye.

title: Dubai on a budget: free sights, metro tips and the best time to visit
desc: Dubai doesn't have to be expensive: when to go, how to get around and which attractions are worth paying for.
body:
Dubai is known for luxury, but many of its best experiences are free or cheap, and the metro makes getting around easy.

When to go

November to March is pleasantly warm. Summer (June to September) is extremely hot but brings big hotel discounts – plan indoor activities and go out in the evening.

Free and cheap experiences

  • The Dubai Fountain show at the foot of the Burj Khalifa, every evening.
  • Old Dubai: Al Fahidi historical district, the souks, and an abra (water taxi) across the Creek for a small fare.
  • Public beaches such as JBR and Kite Beach.
  • Dubai Marina walk at sunset.

Worth paying for

The Burj Khalifa observation decks, a desert safari, and the Museum of the Future are popular – booking online is usually cheaper than at the door, and popular time slots sell out.

Getting around

The metro runs from the airport (Terminals 1 and 3) along the main road to the Marina. A Nol card is needed; the Gold class costs extra. For a quick ride from the airport, a pre-booked transfer is fixed-price. Renting a car is useful for trips to Abu Dhabi or Hatta.

Money tips

  • Alcohol is expensive; food courts and Indian or Pakistani restaurants in Deira and Karama are great value.
  • Stay near a metro station to save on taxis.

title: Bangkok first trip: temples, food and getting around
desc: Where to stay in Bangkok, how to use the river boats and Skytrain, and how to avoid common scams.
body:
Bangkok is intense, delicious and surprisingly affordable. A bit of planning helps you skip the traffic and the touts.

Where to stay

  • Sukhumvit – on the BTS Skytrain, with lots of hotels and restaurants.
  • Riverside – close to the boats and the old city sights.
  • Silom – business district with night markets and good transport links.

Top sights

  • The Grand Palace and Wat Phra Kaew – dress code applies (covered shoulders and knees).
  • Wat Pho with the reclining Buddha, and Wat Arun across the river.
  • Chatuchak Weekend Market and the canals (khlongs) of Thonburi.

Getting around

Use the BTS Skytrain and MRT metro to beat traffic, and the Chao Phraya Express boats for riverside sights. From Suvarnabhumi Airport, the Airport Rail Link reaches the city in about 30 minutes; a private transfer is simpler late at night.

Avoid common scams

  • If someone says a sight is "closed today" and offers a tuk-tuk tour, politely decline.
  • Use metered taxis or ride-hailing apps; agree on the price before a tuk-tuk ride.

Plan ahead

Day trips to Ayutthaya, the floating markets or a Thai cooking class can be booked online. Stay connected with an eSIM for Thailand, and compare flights to Bangkok across airlines.

title: Tenerife in winter: where to stay for sun and how to keep costs down
desc: Why Tenerife is Europe's favourite winter sun escape, which side of the island to choose, and how to save on flights, transfers and trips to Mount Teide.
body:
When most of Europe is grey, the Canary Islands still see mild temperatures and plenty of sunshine, which is why Tenerife is one of the most popular winter escapes on the continent. It is part of Spain and the EU, so the euro, EU roaming rules and EU flight rights all apply.

North or south?

  • The south (Costa Adeje, Los Cristianos, Playa de las Américas) is the driest and sunniest side, with most beaches and resort hotels. Best if sun is the priority.
  • The north (Puerto de la Cruz, La Orotava) is greener, cooler and cloudier, with more local life and often lower prices.
  • Santa Cruz, the capital, suits travellers who want a real city with shops and restaurants.

Getting there and around

Tenerife has two airports: Tenerife South (TFS), closest to the resorts, and Tenerife North (TFN), mostly for flights from mainland Spain and the other islands. Winter weeks around Christmas and school holidays sell out early, so compare flight dates early. Public buses (TITSA) cover the island well; a pre-booked transfer is easier with luggage, and to explore the volcanic interior at your own pace you can rent a car.

What to do

  • Mount Teide: Spain's highest peak and a national park. The cable car is popular, so book tickets in advance; going to the summit itself needs a free permit booked well ahead.
  • Whale and dolphin watching from the south coast.
  • Masca village and its gorge, and the cliffs of Los Gigantes.
  • Stargazing: the island's skies are among the clearest in Europe.

Money-saving tips

  • Apartments with a kitchen are often cheaper than all-inclusive hotels for longer stays.
  • Eat in local guachinches (simple family restaurants in the north) rather than on the beachfront.
  • Mid-January to early February is usually cheaper than the Christmas period.

title: Antalya: old town, beaches and day trips on a budget
desc: A practical guide to Antalya on the Turkish Riviera: where to stay, Kaleiçi old town, beaches, ancient sites and how to get from the airport.
body:
Antalya is the gateway to the Turkish Riviera. Most visitors arrive for beach holidays in nearby resorts such as Belek, Side, Kemer and Alanya, but the city itself has a charming walled old town, waterfalls and some of the best-preserved ancient sites in the Mediterranean.

Where to stay

  • Kaleiçi – the historic old town with boutique hotels in Ottoman houses, close to the old harbour.
  • Konyaaltı – a long pebble beach west of the centre with modern hotels and a seaside promenade.
  • Lara – sandy beaches east of the city and large all-inclusive resorts, near the airport.

Getting around

Antalya Airport (AYT) is about 15 km from the centre. Trams and city buses connect the airport, Lara, the centre and Konyaaltı. For resorts further away, a pre-booked transfer saves haggling with taxis. Summer is peak season; spring and autumn are warm, cheaper and less crowded, so compare flight prices across several weeks.

What to see

  • Hadrian's Gate, the Yivli Minaret and the lanes of Kaleiçi.
  • Düden and Kurşunlu waterfalls, easy half-day trips.
  • Ancient cities: Perge, Aspendos (with its huge Roman theatre) and Termessos in the mountains.
  • Boat trips along the coast from the old harbour.

Guided trips to the ancient sites and boat excursions are easy to book online, and a car is the cheapest way to see several sites in one day if you are a group – you can compare car rental prices.

Tips

  • Agree the price before taking a taxi or use official taxi stands.
  • Bazaar prices are negotiable; supermarkets are much cheaper for water and snacks.
  • Get mobile data before you land with an eSIM – roaming outside the EU can be expensive.

title: Hurghada: Red Sea holiday guide – snorkelling, resorts and day trips
desc: How to plan a good-value Red Sea holiday in Hurghada: the best areas, snorkelling and diving, trips to Luxor and practical tips on visas and transfers.
body:
Hurghada is one of Egypt's main Red Sea resorts, known for warm sea temperatures much of the year, coral reefs close to shore and many package holidays from Europe. It is a popular winter sun option because it stays warm when Europe is cold.

Where to stay

  • Sahl Hasheesh and Makadi Bay – quieter bays south of the city with resort hotels and good house reefs.
  • El Gouna – a lagoon town north of Hurghada with a marina and a more independent feel.
  • Hurghada city (Sekalla, the marina) – cheaper hotels, local restaurants and boat departures.

Before you go

  • Most visitors need a visa; many nationalities can get one on arrival or online. Check the current rules for your passport before booking.
  • Package holidays (flight + hotel) are often cheaper than booking separately here – compare both, and check flight prices for your dates.
  • A pre-booked airport transfer avoids negotiating with drivers on arrival.

Things to do

  • Snorkelling and diving trips to Giftun Island and nearby reefs.
  • Day trips to Luxor's temples and the Valley of the Kings – a long day, but unforgettable.
  • Desert safaris by jeep or quad, often with a Bedouin dinner.

Choose licensed operators and read what is included before you book excursions. Tours sold on the beach can be cheaper but quality varies a lot.

Tips

  • Bring reef-safe sunscreen and never touch or stand on coral.
  • Small cash in euros, dollars or Egyptian pounds is useful for tips.
  • Set up an eSIM before travelling to avoid high roaming charges.

title: Budapest on a budget: baths, views and ruin bars
desc: How to enjoy Budapest without overspending: where to stay, the thermal baths, free viewpoints, transport passes and food tips.
body:
Budapest is two cities in one: hilly Buda with the castle on one bank of the Danube and lively Pest with grand boulevards on the other. It is still one of the better-value capitals in Central Europe, especially if you follow a few simple rules.

Where to stay

  • District V (Belváros) – central, walkable, near the river and the Parliament.
  • District VII (Jewish Quarter) – ruin bars, cafés and nightlife; can be noisy.
  • District VIII and IX – cheaper and well connected by metro and tram.

Getting around

Buy a 24-hour, 72-hour or weekly travel card instead of single tickets; it covers metro, trams and buses, including tram 2 along the Danube, one of the most scenic rides in Europe. The 100E airport bus runs to the centre; a pre-booked transfer is easier late at night.

What to see for free or cheap

  • Walk up to Fisherman's Bastion and the Castle District; the lower terraces are free.
  • Gellért Hill for the best panoramic view of the city.
  • Margaret Island, the Central Market Hall and the Shoes on the Danube Bank memorial.

Thermal baths

Széchenyi and Gellért are the famous ones, while smaller baths are often cheaper and less crowded. Weekday mornings are the quietest. Bath entry and Danube cruises can be booked online to skip the queues.

Food and money tips

  • Pay in forints and choose to be charged in local currency on card terminals.
  • Look for lunch menus (napi menü) on weekdays – a soup and main for much less than dinner prices.
  • Check that a service charge is not already on the bill before tipping.

title: A weekend in Kraków: Old Town, Wawel and day trips
desc: A 2–3 day plan for Kraków: Old Town and Wawel Castle, Kazimierz, how to visit Auschwitz-Birkenau and the Wieliczka Salt Mine, and budget tips.
body:
Kraków escaped major destruction in the Second World War, so its medieval Old Town, one of Europe's largest market squares and Wawel Castle survive largely intact. It is compact, affordable and easy to reach on low-cost flights.

Day 1: Old Town and Wawel

Start at the Main Market Square with the Cloth Hall and St Mary's Basilica, where a trumpet call is played every hour from the tower. Walk down the Royal Route to Wawel Hill for the castle and cathedral. In the evening, the Planty park ring around the Old Town is pleasant for a walk.

Day 2: Kazimierz and Podgórze

Kazimierz, the historic Jewish quarter, has synagogues, cafés and lively bars. Cross the river to Podgórze for Schindler's Factory museum, which tells the story of the city under occupation.

Day trips

  • Auschwitz-Birkenau Memorial – about 1.5 hours away. Entry is controlled by timed passes that run out in high season, so plan ahead; guided visits are recommended.
  • Wieliczka Salt Mine – underground chapels carved from salt, about 30 minutes from the centre.
  • Zakopane and the Tatra Mountains for a mountain day.

You can book tickets and tours online or take an audio guide for the Old Town and go at your own pace.

Practical tips

  • Trains run from Kraków Airport to the main station in under 20 minutes.
  • Pay in złoty and choose local currency on card terminals.
  • Milk bars (bar mleczny) serve traditional Polish food at very low prices.
  • Low-cost airlines fly here from across Europe – compare dates to find the cheapest weekend.

title: Paris for first-timers: where to stay, what to book and how to save
desc: A practical first-time guide to Paris: the best areas to stay, which sights to book in advance, transport tips and free things to do.
body:
Paris rewards a little planning. The famous sights need booking, the metro makes everything close, and many of the best experiences – walking along the Seine, markets, parks – cost nothing.

Where to stay

  • Le Marais (3rd/4th) – central, historic and lively, full of cafés and small museums.
  • Saint-Germain and the Latin Quarter (5th/6th) – classic Left Bank charm, close to Notre-Dame.
  • Canal Saint-Martin and the 11th – younger, more local and often cheaper.
  • Montmartre (18th) – village feel and views, but hilly and further from the centre.

Book in advance

  • The Louvre requires timed entry; mornings and late openings are calmer.
  • The Eiffel Tower summit sells out on busy days.
  • Sainte-Chapelle, Musée d'Orsay and Versailles also have timed tickets.

Reserve the main sights online here so you don't spend your trip in queues.

Getting around

The metro and RER cover the city and both main airports. Check the current ticket options before you go, as the fare system has changed in recent years. A pre-booked transfer from Charles de Gaulle or Orly is easier with children or luggage.

Free and cheap

  • Many national museums are free on the first Sunday of some months, and free for EU residents under 26.
  • Walk the Seine banks, Île de la Cité and Île Saint-Louis, and the Tuileries and Luxembourg gardens.
  • Sacré-Cœur and the steps of Montmartre for a free view over the city.
  • Picnic with bread, cheese and fruit from a local market instead of eating near the big sights.
